'''Joan Hinton''' ([[Chinese language|Chinese]] name: 寒春, [[Pinyin]]: ''Hán Chūn''; 20 October 1921 – 8 June 2010)<ref name="nytimes_dead"/> was a [[nuclear physicist]] and one of the few female scientists who worked for the [[Manhattan Project]] in [[Los Alamos National Laboratory|Los Alamos]]. Dismayed at the use of the atomic bomb against the Japanese, she went to live and work in China, staying on after the establishment of the [[People's Republic of China]] after 1949. She and her husband [[Erwin Engst|Erwin (Sid) Engst]] participated in China's efforts at developing a socialist economy, working extensively in agriculture, and supported the policies of [[Mao Zedong]]. She lived on a dairy farm north of [[Beijing]] before her death on June 8, 2010.

== Early life ==
On October 20, 1921, Hinton was born as Joan Chase Hinton in [[Chicago]], [[Illinois]].<ref name="nytimes_dead">Grimes, William. June 11, 2010. {{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2010/06/12/science/12hinton.html | title= ''Joan Hinton, Physicist Who Chose China Over Atom Bomb, Is Dead at 88'' nytimes.com |newspaper=[[The New York Times]] | date= 12 June 2010 |accessdate= Dec 18, 2016| last1= Grimes | first1= William }}</ref> Her father, Sebastian Hinton, was a lawyer (who also was the inventor of the [[jungle gym]]<ref>Hinton's original patents for the "climbing structure" are {{US patent|1471465}} filed July 22, 1920; {{US patent|1488244}} filed October 1, 1920; {{US patent|1488245}} filed October 1, 1920; and {{US patent|1488246}} filed October 24, 1921.</ref>); her mother, [[Carmelita Hinton]], was an educator and the founder of [[The Putney School]], an independent progressive school in [[Vermont]].

=== Family background ===
Joan Hinton's great-grandfather was the mathematician [[George Boole]], and her grandfather was the mathematician [[Charles Howard Hinton]]. [[Ethel Lilian Voynich]], a great-aunt, was the author of ''[[The Gadfly]]'', a novel later read by millions of Soviet and Chinese readers. Her sister, Jean Hinton Rosner (1917–2002), was a civil rights and peace activist. She was first cousin, once removed, with [[Geoffrey Hinton]].

== Education ==
Hinton graduated from the Putney School, where her skiing skills qualified her for a berth on the 1940 [[U.S. Ski Team]] at the [[Winter Olympic Games]], had they been held that year. She studied physics at [[Bennington College]] and graduated in 1942 with a bachelor's degree in natural science. In 1944, Hinton earned a doctorate in physics from [[University of Wisconsin]].<ref name="nytimes_dead"/><ref>{{cite book | author=Ruth H. Howes | author-link=Ruth Howes|author2=Caroline L. Herzenberg
| author2-link=Caroline Herzenberg|publisher=Temple University Press | year = 2003| title=Their Day in the Sun: Women of the Manhattan Project | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Ys0N4rFgt6UC&pg=PA51 | page=51| isbn=9781592131921}}</ref>

== Career ==
=== Nuclear scientist ===
Hinton was in Los Alamos for the Manhattan Project. Under the supervision of [[Enrico Fermi]], she calibrated neutron detectors to be used in the [[Alamogordo, New Mexico|Alamogordo]] test.<ref>E. Segrè, Enrico Fermi, Physicist. University of Chicago Press, Chicago, 1970. Page 145</ref>

She snuck in to watch the [[Trinity test]]; as she recalled:

<blockquote>It was like being at the bottom of an ocean of light. We were bathed in it from all directions. The light withdrew into the bomb as if the bomb sucked it up. Then it turned purple and blue and went up and up and up. We were still talking in whispers when the cloud reached the level where it was struck by the rising sunlight so it cleared out the natural clouds. We saw a cloud that was dark and red at the bottom and daylight on the top. Then suddenly the sound reached us. It was very sharp and rumbled and all the mountains were rumbling with it.<ref>https://web.archive.org/web/20230114005024/https://ahf.nuclearmuseum.org/ahf/key-documents/trinity-test-eyewitnesses/</ref><ref>{{cite book | author=Ruth H. Howes | author-link=Ruth Howes|author2=Caroline L. Herzenberg
| author2-link=Caroline Herzenberg|publisher=Temple University Press | year = 2003| title=Their Day in the Sun: Women of the Manhattan Project | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Ys0N4rFgt6UC&pg=PA51 | page=51, 56| isbn=9781592131921}}</ref></blockquote>

Joan Hinton was shocked when the US government, three weeks later, dropped [[nuclear bomb]]s on [[Hiroshima]] and [[Nagasaki, Nagasaki|Nagasaki]]. She left the Manhattan Project and lobbied the government in [[Washington, D.C.|Washington]] to internationalize [[nuclear power]].

=== Moving to China ===
Her brother [[William H. Hinton]] (1919–2004) had travelled to China for the first time in 1937 and returned after the war. His book ''[[Fanshen|Fanshen: Documentary of Revolution in a Chinese Village]]'', published in 1966 described his observations of [[land reform]] in the [[Communist-controlled China (1927–1949)|communist-occupied area]] of Northwest China. With his advice, in March 1948, Joan Hinton travelled to Shanghai, worked for [[Soong Ching-ling]], the widow of President [[Sun Yat-sen]], and tried to establish contacts with the Chinese communists. She witnessed the communists gaining control of Beijing in 1949 and moved to [[Yan'an]], where she married Erwin Engst, who had been working in China since 1946. After 5 months living in caves in 1949 they moved to the [[Yan'an Soviet|border]] of [[Suiyuan]] to work on a state farm called Sanbien Farm,<ref>The name literally means "three borders", and is in fact a combination of the names of [[Dingbian|Dingbien]], {{Interlanguage link|Anbian, Dingbian County|lt=Anbian|zh|安边镇 (定边县)}} and [[Jingbian|Jingbien]] of which the farm located at the border. </ref> living meagerly in a stockaded village named Chungchuan<ref>Now a town in [[Otog Front Banner]], [[Ordos City|Ordos]]. </ref> without electricity or radios. At one point the village was attacked by bandits. No one knew in the U.S. of their whereabouts except family and  a circle of scientists. In October 1952 Joan went public in Beijing, attending the [[Asia and Pacific Rim Peace Conference]] where she denounced the [[Atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki|atomic bombing of Hiroshima]].<ref>{{cite|first=Gerry |last=Kennedy |title=The Booles and the Hintons: Two Dynasties That Helped Shape the Modern World |publisher= Attic Press |year=2017|isbn= 978-1782051855}}</ref> She was called "The Atom Spy Who Got Away", and questions were asked about her and her brother William during the [[Army–McCarthy hearings]], but she never used her scientific training in China's nuclear program. In May 1955, she, Erwin, and their three young children moved to a farm near [[Xi'an]]. In April 1966 the family moved to Beijing to work as translators and editors at the beginning of the [[Cultural Revolution]].{{sfnb|Cheng|2026}}{{sfnb|Hayford|2010}}

After 1956, Hinton finally obtained permanent residency to live in China and she chose to retain her US citizenship.<ref name="shanghaiist_residentofchina">Dec 18, 2015. {{cite web|url=http://shanghaiist.com/2015/12/18/laowai_chinese.php| title= ''Laowai Chinese: The elite few foreigners who have managed to obtain permanent residency in China'' shanghaiist.com |accessdate= Dec 18, 2016}}</ref>

On August 29 (or in June, according to another source), 1966, Joan, Erwin and two other Americans living in China—[[Bertha Sneck]] (''Shǐ Kè'' 史克, who had previously been married to Joan's brother William) and Ann Tompkins (''Tāngpǔjīnsēn'' 汤普金森)—signed a [[big-character poster]] put up at the Foreign Experts Bureau in Beijing with the following text:{{citation needed|date=March 2020}}
<blockquote>Which monsters and freaks are pulling the strings so foreigners get this kind of treatment? Foreigners working in China, no matter what class background they have, no matter what their attitude is toward the revolution, they all get the "five nots and two haves": the five nots—first: no physical labour, second: no thought reform, third: no chances of contacts with workers and peasants, fourth: no participation in class struggle, fifth: no participation in production struggle; the two haves—first: they have an exceptionally high living standard, second: they have all kinds of specialization. What kind of concept is that? This is [[Nikita Khrushchev|Khrushchev]]ism, this is revisionist thinking, this is class exploitation! [...] We demand: [...] Seventh: the same living standard and the same level of Chinese staff; eighth: no specialization any more. Long live the Great Proletarian Cultural Revolution!</blockquote>

A copy of the poster was shown to [[Mao Zedong]], who issued a directive that "revolutionary foreign experts and their children should be treated the same as the Chinese."<ref>{{cite book |author1=Mao Zedong |title=建国以来毛泽东文稿第十二册 |trans-title=Manuscripts of Mao Zedong since the Founding of the People's Republic |date=8 September 1966 |page=126 |publisher=Central Party Literature Press ([[Central Literature Publishing House]]) |url=https://www.marxists.org/chinese/pdf/chinese_marxists/mao/c12.pdf |accessdate=21 March 2020 |language=Chinese |chapter=对四位美国专家的一张大字报的批语 |trans-chapter=Remarks on the Big Character Poster Written by the Four America Specialists}}</ref>

In 1972, Joan and Erwin started working in agriculture again at the Red Star Commune in [[Daxing, Beijing|Daxing]], [[Beijing]]. In June 1987, William Hinton went to the town of [[Dazhai, Xiyang County|Dazhai]] in [[Shanxi]] province to observe the changes brought about by the reform policies, and in August 1987, Joan Hinton stayed at Dazhai as well.{{citation needed|date=March 2020}}

In a 1996 interview with [[CNN]], after nearly 50 years in China, she stated "[we] never intended to stay in China so long, but were too caught up to leave."<ref name="CNN">Andrea Koppel: [http://www.cnn.com/WORLD/9610/01/china.us.reds/ Leftist Americans in China grieve shift to capitalism] (''CNN'', October 1st, 1996)—with photo of Sid Engst and Hinton</ref> Hinton described the changes she and her husband had witnessed in China since the beginning of the [[reform and opening up]] of Deng Xiaoping in the late 1970s.  They stated they "have watched their socialist dream fall apart" as much of China embraced capitalism. A 2004 [[MSNBC]] interview noted her critical assessment of economic change as "betrayals of the socialist cause."<ref name="NBC">[[Catherine Rampell]]: [https://web.archive.org/web/20161220205851/http://www.nbcnews.com/id/5653644/ The atom spy that got away] American defector to Maoist China not happy with 56 years of progress (''NBC'', August 13th, 2004)</ref> She noted what she describes as a rise of exploitation in Chinese society.

Hinton lived alone following the death of her husband in 2003. Her three children moved to the United States, with Hinton noting that "They probably would have stayed if China were still socialist." Hinton retained her American citizenship, which she considered "convenient for travel."<ref name="NBC" /> Her son, Yang Heping (Fred Engst) moved back to Beijing in 2007 as a professor at the [[University of International Business and Economics (Beijing)|University of International Business and Economics]].<ref>[http://site.uibe.edu.cn/newsenglish/html/ViewNewsInfo.aspx?sysName=TradeSchoolTeacher&NewsId=265 "Yang, Heping's page in the faculty pages"] . Retrieved: 14 October 2014.</ref>

In her 2005 essay "The Second Superpower",<ref>Joan Hinton: [http://peace.blogsport.eu/issues/the-second-superpower The Second Superpower] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211206152638/http://peace.blogsport.eu/issues/the-second-superpower |date=2021-12-06 }} (Beijing International Peace Vigil)</ref> Hinton stated, "There are two opposing superpowers in the world today: the U.S. on one side, and world public opinion on the other. The first thrives on war. The second demands peace and social justice."

She remained active in the small community of expats in Beijing, protesting against the [[2003 invasion of Iraq|war in Iraq]].

== Personal life ==
In 1949, Hinton married [[Erwin Engst]] (1919–2003), a dairy-cattle expert, in [[Yan'an]], [[Shaanxi| Shaanxi Province]], China.<ref name="nytimes_dead"/> Hinton had two sons, Bill and Fred Engst and a daughter, Karen Engst.<ref name="nytimes_dead"/>
In 1923 Hinton's father checked himself into a clinic for treatment, but while there he committed suicide.<ref name="Founding Mothers">{{cite book |title=Founding Mothers and Others: Women Educational Leaders During the Progressive Era |last=Lloyd |first=Susan McIntosh |chapter=Carmelita Chase Hinton and the Putney School |pages=[https://archive.org/details/foundingmotherso0000unse/page/111 111–123] |editor1-first=Alan R. |editor1-last=Sadovnik |editor2-first=Susan F. |editor2-last=Semel |publisher=Palgrave |year=2002 |isbn=0-312-29502-2 |chapter-url=https://archive.org/details/foundingmotherso0000unse/page/111 }}</ref>

On June 8, 2010, Hinton died in [[Beijing]], China. She was 88.<ref name="nytimes_dead"/>
